t: Count Subarrays With K Distinct Integers, Each Appearing at Least m Times
o: Count subarrays with exactly k distinct values where every distinct value occurs at least m times. For a fixed right end r, validity is monotone in the left end: growing the window raises both the distinct count and every frequency, so the valid left endpoints form a contiguous range, countable with three independent two-pointer sweeps.
k: For fixed r: distinct(l..r) is non-increasing in l, so 'exactly k distinct' is an interval [l1, l0-1] found by two at-most-k / at-most-(k-1) pointers.
All-frequencies->=m is also monotone in window size, so a third pointer G gives the largest valid left end; the answer contribution is the intersection length.
All three pointers only move forward, giving O(n) total.

a.i: Maintain l1 = smallest l with distinct(l..r) <= k, l0 = smallest l with distinct(l..r) <= k-1 (so exactly-k holds for l in [l1, l0-1]), and G = largest l such that every value in [l..r] occurs >= m times (shrink G while the decremented count is 0 or still >= m). Intersect the ranges.
s: Per r, add nums[r] to three separate count maps.
Advance l1 while distinct > k; advance l0 while distinct > k-1.
Advance G while dropping nums[G] leaves its count at 0 or >= m.
Add max(0, min(l0-1, r) - max(l1, G) + 1).
a.t: O(n) — each of the three pointers advances at most n times total

w: The crux is proving the valid-left-endpoints set is an interval: both the distinct count and the minimum frequency are monotone under window growth. Verify on example 1 (only [0..3] and [0..4] qualify) and example 2 (m=1 reduces to classic exactly-k). Pitfalls: mixing the three count maps, and off-by-one on the [l1, l0-1] interval. Follow-up: m given per-value, or counting with at most k distinct.
